Private equity cannot rely on cheap debt and rising market prices anymore.
With higher interest rates, returns come from one thing only: making portfolio companies run better.

Many operators thought AI would be an easy shortcut. The data says otherwise:
• 95 percent of corporate AI projects fail to produce real profit (MIT).
• Only 6 percent of private equity firms see major gains in daily operations today (McKinsey).
• 40 percent of buyers discount acquisition offers by 5 percent or more for messy tech (BCG).

If you are an operating partner , here is the six step playbook to turn software into actual cash earnings:

Test claims strictly before buying
Apply a pass or fail test during diligence. If a company cannot prove daily production, clear ownership, verified math, full cloud running costs, and safe data access, remove those promised savings from your purchase price.

Count real cash only
Real profit equals actual money saved minus new computer bills. Only count payroll savings when real jobs or outside contracts end. Never count avoided future hiring as Day 1 profit.

Fix core systems in the first 100 days
Do not put smart automation on top of broken software. Spend the first 100 days cleaning customer records, upgrading core accounting databases, and killing shared passwords.

Start in the finance department
Enforce a six month payback rule. If a project cannot prove cash gains in two quarters, kill it. Finance is the best entry point because accounting numbers are clean, audited, and show direct dollar savings fast.

Use four checkpoints to stop failing tests
Most companies fail because they never cancel bad projects. Enforce four gates: Admit, Validate, Build, and Copy. If a pilot fails to prove its value quickly, shut it down.

Track running costs and secure logins
Model fees and cloud computing add up fast. Track bills down to the specific task so software costs do not eat your margins. Give every automated tool its own secure account and an emergency off switch.


Stop treating AI like an open ended experiment. 
Fix your basic data, track every dollar of running costs, kill failing pilots early, and turn technology into verified operating profit.

[Generational Predicament] Graduating from university doesn't mean finding a job! 26-year-old unemployed for a year and a half laments facing a "Triple Squeeze," crying Out: "If there aren't even junior positions, how can I build experience?"     (8).

Part II: Executing a high-conversion turnaround with 5W1H.

Once root causes are isolated, deploying the 5W1H strategic framework (What, Why, Who, Where, When, and How) transforms a chaotic job search into a precision campaign.

The turnaround begins by defining "What" exact role and tangible value you are pitching. Instead of presenting yourself as an unfocused generalist willing to take any opening, narrow your target to two or three specific functional tracks—such as project coordination, business analytics, or compliance support—and build a concrete portfolio of case studies or project deliverables that prove day-one readiness. Closely aligned with this is answering "Why" a top employer should select you over hundreds of equally credentialed applicants. Crafting a sharp Unique Value Proposition (UVP)—such as pairing your core discipline with AI workflow automation, bilingual communication, and structured problem-solving—gives hiring managers a compelling commercial reason to interview you.

With positioning locked in, you must identify "Who" holds actual hiring influence and "Where" high-probability openings reside. Bypassing the HR portal black hole requires mapping three key personas on LinkedIn: line department heads, university alumni inside target firms, and specialized recruitment consultants. Simultaneously, expand beyond saturated public job boards into company career portals, industry associations, and six-to-twelve-month agency contract roles—a proven "Trojan Horse" entry strategy that allows top performers to convert into permanent headcount from the inside.

Finally, disciplined execution hinges on mastering "When" to act and "How" to optimize every step of the funnel. Submitting tailored applications within the critical first 48 to 72 hours of a job posting ensures your profile reaches recruiters while their shortlist is still open, while maintaining a sustainable weekly sprint—such as five tailored applications paired with five alumni outreach messages—prevents emotional burnout. Every resume must be calibrated with role-specific ATS keywords, every interview backed by quantified STAR-method stories, and every stage of the pipeline reviewed weekly so bottlenecks are corrected in real time. In an era where entry-level jobs are no longer handed out automatically, graduates who treat their career launch with the rigor of a problem-solving engineer will always outmaneuver the crowd.

Solubility belongs in the brief before a chemist makes the molecule. At Isomorphic Labs, designers give an AI agent the target and desired properties, then use its search to decide which compounds deserve a place in the lab.

Founder and CEO Demis Hassabis and President Max Jaderberg now have a $5B Series C behind that work. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital co-led the November 17 round, joined by Andreessen Horowitz, Alphabet Inc., Thrive Capital, MGX, GV (Google Ventures), CapitalG, Temasek and the UK Sovereign AI Fund, alongside other new investors. The announcement did not disclose a valuation.

The London company's IsoDDE drug design engine brings predictive and generative models into the same process. Its researchers can explore designs computationally, refine their properties, then select compounds to synthesize and test. In a September example, Isomorphic described an agent working over 2-4 days before selected designs went into laboratory testing. That clock measures a computational search, not the time required to develop a medicine.

The interesting choice is where to put the scientists' effort. An enormous search space becomes more useful when researchers can ask a precise question and get designs worth making. Isomorphic is building the models, generating data and organizing the scientific work around that decision, with internal oncology and immunology programs alongside partnerships with Novartis, Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson.

The company reports positive preclinical results and says the new capital will also support translational and clinical-development infrastructure. CMO Ben Wolf brings clinical leadership into a business whose ambitions now reach well beyond predicting molecular structures. The current hiring board includes clinical contracts and supply-chain roles in Cambridge, Massachusetts, alongside compute and inference positions.

That range of work explains something the round size alone cannot. A team can improve its molecular designs and create more work for the people deciding how to carry them forward. Those people need an organization that can keep up with the engine without treating every promising output as a finished medicine.

Isomorphic raised $2.1B in May after a $600M first external round in March 2025. This latest commitment follows that earlier backing into the lab, where researchers still have to choose the compounds, learn from the experiments and work with clinical colleagues preparing to take candidates further.

Anthropic priced its IPO last night. It sold about 980m shares and raised 81.3bn $, which surpasses SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.

And I bought shares. I mean, I gave this company so much money so far that I got...curious? 
And I sit somewhere in between "this is an AI bubble" and "but what if it is not?".

I learnt, before buying my ginormous 4 shares  🤣 , that nearly a quarter of their 2025 revenue came from 2 customers, and most large clients have no long-term contracts. I also learnt that investors valued it at about 1.5 trillion $, down from roughly 2 trillion $ a week ago (nail biting)

Then, I saw that companies listed in the US reach average valuations more than 3 times higher than their European counterparts. Europe also produces 80% fewer scale-ups and 85% fewer unicorns. So is my thinking biased by the fact that I live in one of the world's most risk adverse countries? Most likely. Otherwise I may have bought 10 shares?  😂 

But still, most of the money I invested is in AI related organisations (think supply chain and co.)

Anyway, I am not an investor, I run a huge Talent community and I am a TA professional. So my interest is less in the bull vs bear markets and more is "how is all of this affecting the workforce?"

Anthropic’s own research with Stanford found entry-level hiring in AI-exposed sectors fell 16% in 2025. Overall unemployment has barely moved, and the change shows up as fewer junior hires. If we keep cutting entry-level roles, in 5 years we will struggle to find anyone ready for the mid-level ones
 
So, lmk...
 
Who fills our mid-level roles in 2031 if we don't hire juniors now?
Do we know what we spend on AI tools, and what we get back?
Are we deciding AI budget and headcount together, or separately?

DATA CENTER OPERATIONS: COMMISSIONING THE FACILITY IS ONLY THE BEGINNING.

A hyperscale AI data center can pass L1–L5 commissioning and Integrated Systems Testing (IST).

But what happens the day after turnover?

That is where the Director of Data Center Operations becomes accountable.

Construction delivers the infrastructure. Commissioning verifies its performance. Operations must sustain that performance 24/7 while equipment ages, workloads change, maintenance occurs, and failures happen.

A director is not there to personally operate every breaker, repair every chiller, or write every MOP.

The job is to build and lead the organization that keeps the facility safe, available, and financially controlled.

WHAT DOES THAT REQUIRE?

1. RELIABILITY: Monitor critical loads, redundancy, alarms, and degraded operating conditions. A facility can be online and still be one failure away from an outage.

2. PEOPLE: Maintain qualified 24/7 staffing, clear escalation authority, training, and shift accountability.

3. MAINTENANCE: Control preventive maintenance, asset condition, spare parts, OEM support, and deferred-work risks.

4. PROCEDURES: Govern SOPs, MOPs, EOPs, switching activities, and changes to live systems.

5. INCIDENT RESPONSE: Establish command, stabilize operations, communicate impacts, recover safely, and address root causes.

6. CAPACITY AND COOLING: Track electrical headroom, IT load, chilled-water performance, CDU availability, flow, temperature, and thermal redundancy.

7. BUSINESS PERFORMANCE: Manage OpEx, CapEx, vendor contracts, customer commitments, and measurable operating KPIs.

HERE IS THE EXECUTION GAP.

Too many organizations treat substantial completion or successful IST as proof that the facility is operationally ready.

It is not enough.

Before accepting turnover, operations needs approved procedures, trained personnel, verified alarms, accurate as-builts, maintenance plans, critical spares, closed high-risk deficiencies, and documented ownership of remaining risks.

A generator that passed its load-bank test can still fail months later.

A CDU that passed functional testing can still develop a flow or water-quality problem.

A UPS can support the load while its redundancy is compromised.

THE DIRECTOR MUST IDENTIFY THE RISK BEFORE THE CUSTOMER EXPERIENCES THE OUTAGE.

THE REAL DIFFERENCE:

Commissioning asks: Does the system perform as designed?

Operations asks: Can we keep it performing safely, reliably, and efficiently every single day?

DATA CENTER OWNERS: ARE YOU HIRING OPERATIONS DIRECTORS TO MANAGE FACILITIES OR SIMPLY TO REACT WHEN SOMETHING BREAKS?

A recruiting tool launched this week promising to go from job description to booked interview in under five minutes, running "autonomously, 24x7," no contract needed. Its pitch line stuck with me: hiring at the speed AI now writes code, in minutes instead of months.

We have run our own hiring agent at Sunday for thirteen weeks, held to the same 90-day bar as a new human hire. The fastest thing we built in that stretch is also the one I regret most.

Early on we let it shortlist candidates off one automated call, no human listening in, to cut shortlist time in half. It worked, for a while. Then a hiring manager caught it waving through someone who had clearly rehearsed answers off a script, the kind of thing a recruiter catches from tone alone in ninety seconds. We put a human back in that loop. Shortlist time went right back up.

So when a company advertises an agent running that fast with nobody checking in, I believe the speed. I don't yet believe the accuracy comes free with it.

Maybe I'm wrong, and five minutes is enough once the model is good enough. Where would you draw the line between automating a hiring step and still needing a human inside it?
